paragraphs.text: A letter urging the translation of this book, which is a commentary on the Psalms, from Greek into Syriac. ✝ To the God-loving abbot Simeon of the monastery of Beth Licinius on the Black Mountain, from Barlahe, a sinner and an insignificant man, enclosed in the precinct of Mar Elisha [?]. Greetings in Jesus our Lord, the light of the world and the hope of the dead and the living. First, my lord, we ask after your well-being and beg you to pray for our weakness, that we may [?] from the world and from the temptations of the evil one. We too, my lord, as [?] our lowliness, pray for you, for everyone with you, and for everything you have, that the Lord God, who loves humanity and cares for the life of his creation, may grant you mercy before him, rescue you from the evil world and from the temptations of the enemy, and make you worthy of mercy and compassion at that hour when mercy is needed. Yes and amen. ✝ I inform your loving self that the God-loving reverend deacon Damian came and told us about your love and your zeal for the fear of God. We thanked our Lord on your behalf, that in his mercy he may bring his grace in you to completion until the end. Yes and amen. We also inform your loving selves that he had with him a gathering of ten leaves containing the words of the introduction preceding the commentary on the Psalms by the blessed Athanasius, patriarch of Alexandria the Great. We received its completion [?], and now we long for the commentary on its verses. But for our Lord's sake, if it is easy for you—even if it is only one prophet or two—[?] and translate it, remembering the words of our Lord, who said, “Who is the [?]” “faithful and wise, whom his master will appoint over his household to give his servants their provisions at the proper time?” And again, those talents concerning which the master of the house charged his servants to show their profits. And again, what our Lord said to your namesake: “Feed my sheep, my lambs, and my ewes.” And again: “Blessed is the [?] because of whom his master's name is glorified.” And again: “You are the light of the world and the salt of the earth.” And again: “Whatever you did for one of these little ones, you did for me.” And again: “Strap on your swords and cross over ahead of your brothers until they inherit the land that the Lord God has given them.”

of the nations; for the transformation through the faith of the mind; after this, for Israel; for the honors that will finally belong to the saints; for the city above; for the course toward the corruption of bodies that come from the earth. And, quite simply, once and for all, everything that contributes to benefit and salvation is appropriate for those who encounter it. This is clearly and unmistakably the intention expressed, as though from the Holy Spirit, by the holy Basil, bishop of Caesarea, in the discourse he delivered on the first three verses of “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the way of the wicked.” All Scripture is from the Holy Spirit and is helpful. It was written for this purpose through the prompting of the Spirit of God: that, as from a public hospital, all people might find in the Holy Scriptures healing for the suffering caused by their sins. For truly, the healing that comes from them relieves us of the pain of sins. Now the instruction by which we are trained through the prophets is one thing; the accounts of events in Judges and the Book of Kings take another form; the admonition in the Law belongs to another category; and the proverbs and riddles in the Wisdom of Solomon have another character. Although the fear of God is expressed in all of them in various ways, their accounts differ from one another. But in the book of the holy Psalms, the help supplied by all the books is gathered together, and the meaning of them all is expressed in it. For it prophesies things to come and also recounts things that have happened and been created. The force of the Law is rightly found in it. The deeds of earlier people are also praised in it as they deserve. In short, it is a storehouse of instruction in good things, from which help is available to anyone who takes care to apply it to his sufferings as he seeks it. For through it even the wounds of sins in which we have grown old are healed. Those whose wounds of temptation are just beginning are healed by it. Those who are unharmed are preserved in their righteousness by its warnings. In short, it cleanses the passions of wickedness, however deeply they may be stained into the souls of those who have acquired them. A person can help his soul through the consolation of a fitting and pleasant voice, by directing his thoughts toward pure desire. But because the Holy Spirit saw that the human race is drawn only with difficulty For correction, and because it foresaw [?] in people in the world a contemptible desire for shameful songs, it took beautiful melodies and tunes under the name of the holy psalms and mixed them with the commandments of life, so that they might turn to upright conduct. So that the hearing of our human nature might gently and pleasantly eagerly receive the benefits of the words contained in them, just as wise physicians do for those to whom they wish to [?] harsh medicines for their benefit, mixing them with honey [?] their medicine in a cup with a pungent spice. In this same way, through God's providence, the commandments were combined for us with the beautiful melodies of the psalms, so that, whether people are still young in age or are childish in their understanding of higher things, the word of God might slip into them through songs [?] of their souls. For the word of the apostle and the word of the prophet are easily retained in the memory of the many people today, yet are despised by them because of their plainness. But people eagerly fix the words of the psalms in their memory because of the melodies joined to them, so that it is easy even in houses for them to be sung, repeated in the streets, and recited along the roads in a modest voice. Thus, if someone's anger is like the fury of a wild animal, as soon as he begins to sing, or a song sung by others falls upon his ears, through this very sweet melody he persuades his anger to depart, and easily lulls the harshness of his soul to sleep through it [?]. The psalms, then, are a source of tranquility

for souls and a gift of peace. They calm thoughts when they are disturbed and troubled [?]. For they rouse the soul that has sunk into anger through distress. They are a discipline for those who lack discipline, if they consider what they are singing. For the psalms bring people together in love, draw near those who are far apart, unite those who are divided, and reconcile those who are enemies. For who is not ashamed to have an enemy after raising his voice with the word of God in the holy psalm and saying, “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your kindness,” together with the rest that follows? For the greatest of good things, which is true love, comes about through singing. This was arranged for us so that the many might become one through the praise of the psalms, and from a numerous people one congregation might be formed through harmonious singing. For the psalms truly drive away demons, and the help they give us is like that of the angels. They are a weapon that frees us from fear during terrifying nights. Through meditation on them they are [?] after the toil of the day, in the stillness of the night. For they instruct children through their meditation on them; for the young they bring discipline through the feeling aroused by repeating them. For the elderly they are a delight in [?] recreation, and for women they are a desirable adornment through the good reflection contained in them. Through them the wilderness and its desolation are made peaceful by their holy sound, and through them the streets are made radiant with praise of God. They are the beginning of good study for those who approach God's teaching, and nourishment for those who [?] bear fruit in the practice of righteousness. Through them the steadfastness of the mature is established. They are the sum of the church, its word and its voice, as they thunder among its children. For the psalms, with their melodies, are the splendor and delight of our festivals. And, greatest of all, they produce sorrow for God's sake in anyone who takes on the feeling conveyed by their words. For when they stir feeling, they so move the soul that sings them with understanding that even from a heart of stone they bring sleep at the sight of death [?]. For they are the work of angels and a heavenly way of life among people who devote themselves to them as they sing them. They are spiritual [?], as the prophet who uttered them says: “My prayer is like incense before you.” Oh, the wisdom of the providence of this Lord [?], who arranged for us, as we sing his words, to learn through them what benefits our lives. He devised a way for this to be accomplished in our souls. For teaching imposed by force cannot remain in our understanding without an affection that draws us toward it. But teaching that comes through the beauty of the love of singing clings all the more firmly to our minds, for the building up of our souls. For what is there that you cannot learn from the subjects treated in the psalms? If it is the courage appropriate to striving for good things, you can learn it from them; and if it is care for righteousness, you can hear it from them. And if you seek vigilance in the abundance of its observance, you can find it in them; and if perfection of thought, trained in the order of God, in them [?]; and if how a person should love God, it is interwoven in them; and if [?]. [?] of true repentance, this is [?]. And if the fear of God—what it is like—in them is revealed. And if the measure of endurance—to put it this way, all good things in them are our remedies [?]. And if God should not be exchanged for anything, they proclaim this. And if there is no confidence greater than confidence in him, they persuade us of this. 2. For in the beauty of the Psalms you can find a complete account of the Godhead and of Christ, who appears in the flesh and is God over [?], previously the words concerning him, and their application; and the coming judgment is sternly depicted in them, and the hope of resurrection is boldly written in them, and they justly explain the fear of the punishment that awaits. And the promises of a glorious life are understood through them, and the revelations of glorious mysteries are known through them, and every benefit for the entire human race, in this very book of Psalms, is hidden, so that it may be for everyone a glorious treasury of inexhaustible wealth, through the great treasures within it. As for its being named after all the musical instruments used for song, I think that for this reason the prophet composed and showed us holy music in his words, through the Holy Spirit who played upon him from above. For there was another reason for their producing sound in every melody: the source of sound in all musical instruments is not in those [?] who play them, but rather the beginning of their sound comes from above, except for the lyre and harp, which, through being struck

from below, produce a sound from the bronze of the instrument. But the reason for the prophet’s [?] was God above all [?], where his love was. For in the arrangement of [?], which through its playing prepared for us the music of righteousness for our salvation, we should pursue that higher quest through the practice of the earlier sounds, and not descend toward bodily passions by pursuing the desire for melodies, through the distraction of our hearing, which weakens strength [?]. And there [?] it is drawn away to be harmed. For daily [?], since the [?] of prophecy in music exists for our benefit, as it was profoundly and wisely shown to us in the form of the Gospel’s arrangement, that just as from above is the word of God in the psalm, so we too should grow upward in God. For those who are concerned with the ordering of their souls readily make their way through the Psalms, throughout their lives, among the things above. By Eusebius Pamphili: A discourse on the Psalms, in which he explains what meaning each psalm carries and what its purpose is. The book of Psalms contains new teaching after the Law of Moses. And [?] after the book of Moses, this is a book of instruction. Accordingly, after the end of Moses, of Joshua, and after the judges, this David, as one who was deemed worthy to be himself also the father of the Savior, handed down to the Hebrews this new kind of [?], through his hands [?], showing from these things the legislation given to Moses concerning [?]. But he introduces a new kind of worship of God through praises and loud cries. And the whole work teaches many other things that are withheld from the Law of Moses. 1. “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the way of the wicked.” It teaches zeal and the fear of God, [?] from the opposite. 2. “Why have the nations raged?” A prophecy concerning our peacemaker and the creation of the nations. 3. “Lord, how numerous are my oppressors!” A prophecy of the good things that are to happen to David. 4. “When I called you, you answered me.” A prophecy to David concerning those whom he gathered. 5. “Listen to my words, Lord, and understand my meditation.” A prayer spoken in the person of the church. 5. “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” Instruction in confession. 7. “Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me.” David’s confession and a prophecy concerning the nations. 8. “Lord, our Lord, how glorious is your name in all the earth!” A prophecy of the calling of the nations. 9. “I will give thanks to the Lord with all my heart.” The death of Christ, the resurrection, the receiving of the kingdom, and the destruction of all enemies. 10. “In the Lord I have hoped; how can you say to my soul?” Praise for the victory of the one who fights with God’s help. 11. “Save, Lord, for the good person has disappeared.” An accusation against the wicked and a prophecy concerning the coming of Christ. 12. “How long will you forget me, Lord? Forever?” The enemy's uprising and the expectation of Christ. 13. The wicked man said in his heart, “There is no God.” Concerning the [?] of the evil one and the expectation of Christ. 14. Lord, who will dwell in your tent? Complete restoration in God. 15. Protect me, God, because I have trusted in you. The election of the Church and the resurrection of Christ. 16. Hear, holy Lord, and look upon my petition. The prayer of the perfect man, entirely Christ's, on behalf of those who, because of him, are destined to be saved. 17. I will love you, Lord, my strength and my trust. David's thanksgiving and a prophecy of the [?] of Christ and of the ascension. 18. The heavens declare the glory of God. Discourse on divinity. Divine teaching. 19. May the Lord answer you on the day of distress. The prayer of those who encourage the righteous man. [?] In your strength the king will rejoice. The petition of those who help David. 21. My God, my God, why have you abandoned me? A prophecy of Christ's suffering and the calling of the nations. 22. The Lord will shepherd me, and I will lack nothing. Instruction in the word of the new people. 23. The earth belongs to the Lord, with all that fills it. A prophecy of the calling of the nations and the perfection of those who are saved. 24. To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul. Instruction in confession. 25. Judge me, Lord, because I have walked in my integrity. The petition of one who advances through God. 26. The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? Thanksgiving and a petition for good things. 27. To you, Lord, I have called; my God, do not be silent toward me. A petition together with prophecy. 28. Bring to the Lord, sons of rams. Symbolic prophecy together with discourse on divinity. 29. I will exalt you, Lord, because you have lifted me up. Thanksgiving

together with confession. 30. In you, Lord, I have hoped; may I never be put to shame. Confession together with supplication. 31. Blessed is the one whose wrongdoing has been forgiven. A prophecy of those who are saved through Christ. 32. Praise him, you righteous, the Lord. A command to speak praise, together with discourse on divinity. 33. I will bless the Lord at all times. Instruction in thanksgiving. 34. Lord, plead my case, and fight against those who fight against me. The supplication of the righteous man and a prophecy concerning Christ. 35. The wicked man devises wickedness in his heart. A rebuke of the wicked together with discourse on divinity. 36. Do not envy the wicked. Instruction in the conduct of one who fears God. 37. Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger. Instruction in confession. 38. I said that I would guard my spirit and not sin with my tongue. A petition together with confession. 39. I earnestly hoped in the Lord. The thanksgiving of one who was rescued by God, and a remembrance of the Church. 40. Blessed is the one who considers the poor. A prophecy concerning Christ and concerning the betrayer. 41. Like a deer that cries out for streams of water. The prophet's supplication together with the rejection of the Jewish people. 42. Lord, plead my case and vindicate my claim. The prophet's supplication together with the rejection of the Jewish people. 43. God, we have heard with our ears. The prophet's supplication together with the rejection of the Jewish people. 44. My heart has poured forth a good word. The manifestation of Christ; the kingdom. 45. Our God is our strong refuge. The preaching of the apostles. 46. All you nations, clap your hands. The calling of the nations. 47. Great is our Lord and greatly praised. Praise to God on behalf of the Church, and the destruction of the persecutors. 48. Hear this, all you nations. Instruction concerning divine judgment. 49. God, our God, the Lord, has spoken. The abolition of sacrifices and the law, and the introduction of the law of the new covenant. 50 [?]. Have mercy on me, God, according to your grace. Instruction in confession. 51. Why do you boast of evil, mighty man? A rebuke of an evil way of life and its outcome. 52. The wicked man said in his heart, “There is no God.” A saving revelation and deliverance from godlessness. 53. God, save me by your name. The prayer of one who is persecuted for God's sake. 54. Listen, God, to my prayer, and do not neglect my petition. An account of the things insolently done against Christ. 55. Have mercy on me, God, because a man has trampled me. The thanksgiving of the righteous man who was delivered from enemies. 56. Have mercy on me, God, because my soul hopes in you. Thanksgiving and the calling of the nations. 57. If you truly speak righteousness. Instruction concerning the justice of God's judgment. 58. Rescue me from my enemies, God. The calling of the nations and the rejection of the Jews. 59. God, you have rejected us and driven us away. And you were angry with us. The rejection of the Jewish people and the calling of the nations. 60. Hear my prayer, God, and listen to my petition. A petition with thanksgiving. 61. My soul waits for God, for my salvation comes from him. [?] Healing instruction. 61. My God, you are my God; I will wait for you. Thanksgiving by the one who is perfect in God. 63. Hear my voice, God, when I plead with you. Instruction for the contestant who fears God. 64. Praise is fitting for you, God, in Zion. The calling of the nations and the preaching of the apostles. 65. Praise God, all the earth. The calling of the nations and the preaching of the apostles. 66. May our God have mercy on us. The calling of the nations and the preaching of the apostles. 67. Let God arise, and let all his enemies be scattered. Concerning Christ's becoming human and the calling of the nations. 68. Save me, God, for the waters have reached my soul. Christ's purpose and the rejection of the Jews. 69. God, rescue me; Lord, come to my aid. After the supplication of the righteous and that of Christ. 70. In you, Lord, I have placed my hope; let me never be put to shame. Christ's suffering and resurrection. 71. God, give your judgment to the king. A prophecy of Christ's coming and the calling of the nations. 72. God is good

to Israel and to the pure [?] in heart. An acknowledgment of human weakness concerning the prosperity of the wicked and God's patience. 73. God, why have you forgotten us forever? A prediction of the siege of the city of the Jews, which took place under Vespasian and Titus. 74. We give thanks to you, God. A discourse on Christ's divinity and a reminder of the divine judgment seat. 75. God is known in Judah. The punishment of the wicked by Christ's judgment. 76. I cried aloud to God, and he heard me. Concerning God's patience and his wonderful deeds. 77. My people, listen to my law and be persuaded. Christ's explanation to the church concerning the former people's transgression of the law. 78. God, the nations have entered your inheritance. A prophecy of what happened to the Jews in the days of Antiochus, and an account of the Maccabees. 79. Shepherd of Israel, listen. A prophecy of the siege of the city by the Assyrians, and a petition for Christ's coming. 80. Praise God, who strengthens us. The calling of the nations and instruction concerning what happened to the former people. 81. God stands in the assembly of angels. A rebuke of the wicked among the Jewish people, and a prophecy concerning the nations. 82. God, who is like you? A petition on behalf of the people who suffered afflictions, and a prophecy concerning the end of God's enemies. 83. How lovely are your dwelling places, Lord Almighty. A prophecy concerning Christ and his church. 84. Lord, you showed favor to your land. A prophecy concerning Christ and those who were saved through him. 85. Incline your ear, Lord, and answer me. A prayer of David and a prophecy of the calling of the nations. 86. Its foundations are on his holy mountain. Christ's becoming human and the calling of the nations. 87. Lord, God of my salvation. It foretells Christ's death. 88. I will sing of the Lord's goodness forever. Concerning the kingdom of Christ, who is descended from David. 89. Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout our generations. The rejection of the Jews. 90. He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High. The victory of Christ and of everyone who is made perfect in him. 91. It is good to give thanks to the Lord. Concerning finding rest in God. 92. The Lord reigns and is clothed in majesty. Praise of Christ's kingdom at his first coming. 93. God of vengeance, Lord. Concerning the persecution directed against the church. 94. Come, let us praise the Lord. The calling of the Jews and the cutting off of their hope, though it was their own [?]. 95. Sing a new song to the Lord. The calling of the nations and Christ's coming. 96. The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice. Praise of the kingdom of Christ, and concerning his second coming. 97. Sing a new song to the Lord. The calling of the nations and Christ's coming. 98. The Lord reigns; let the nations tremble. Praise of Christ's kingdom. 99. Praise the Lord, all the earth. Concerning the calling of the nations. 100. I will sing of goodness and justice. Praise by the one who is perfect in God. 101. Lord, hear my prayer. Mourning over the former people, and a prophecy of the new people and the calling of the nations. 102. Bless the Lord, my soul. Instruction in thanksgiving. 103. Bless the Lord, my soul. Instruction in acknowledgment. 104. Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name. Instruction for the nations concerning God's help for the former people. 105. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his goodness lasts forever. Instruction concerning the evil of wickedness. Of the Jews. 106. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his kindness lasts forever. A prophecy of the calling of the nations and God's enlightenment of humanity. 107. My heart is ready, O God. The calling of the nations. 108. O God of my praise, do not be silent. The sufferings of Christ. 109. The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand.” The victory of Christ. 110. I will give thanks to the Lord with all my heart. The thanksgiving of Christ. 111. Blessed is the man who fears the Lord. The calling of the new people and the teaching of Christ. 112. Praise, servants of the Lord. The calling of the new people. 113. When Israel went out from Egypt. The instruction of the new people. 114. I have loved that the Lord should hear the sound of my petition. The progress of the new people. 115. I believed and spoke, and I was greatly humbled. The perfection of the new people. 116. Praise

the Lord, all you nations. The calling of the nations. 114. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his mercies last forever. The victory of those who struggle in Christ, and a prophecy of Christ. 118. Blessed are those whose way is blameless. The beginning of meditation on excellence in God. 119. I called to the Lord in my distress. Concerning life as a sojourner. 120. I will lift my eyes to the mountain. The return from Babylon and the dispersion. 121. I rejoiced when they said to me, The promise of good things. 122. To you I lifted my eyes, you who dwell in heaven. Prayer. 123. If it had not been the Lord who stood by us. Thanksgiving. 124. Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion. Return. 125. When [?] restores the captives of Zion. Expectation of things to come. 126. Unless the Lord builds the house. The [?] of the church. 127. Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord. The calling of the nations. 128. My afflictions have been many since my youth. The victory of service. 129. From the depths I called to you, Lord, and you heard my voice. The prayer of the martyrs. 130. Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been raised high. Concerning humility. 131. Remember David, Lord, and all his humiliation. David's prayer and the revelation of Christ. 132. How good, how pleasant! Concerning the perfected people. 133. Bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord. Instruction in excellence. 134. Praise the name of the Lord. Concerning the people who enter. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his mercies last forever. The thanksgiving of those who were delivered. By the rivers of Babylon. Utterances of the saints who are in captivity. 137. I will give thanks to you, Lord my God, with all my heart. Thanksgiving for prophecy. 138. Lord, you have searched me and known me. Petition. Righteousness. Discourse on the divine nature. 139. Deliver me, Lord, from the evil person. The utterance of one who struggles in God. 140. Lord, I called to you; answer me. The prayer of one who is perfected in God. 141. With my voice I called to the Lord; with my voice I pleaded with the Lord. The utterance of one who is attacked for God's sake. 142. Hear my prayer, Lord, and listen to my petition. The prayer of one who gives thanks. 143. Blessed is the Lord, who taught my hands to fight. The thanksgiving of one who has conquered. 144. I will exalt you, my Lord the King. Praise together with discourse on the divine nature. 145. Praise, my soul, the Lord. Praise together with discourse on the divine nature. 146. It is good to sing to our God, and pleasant. Praise together with discourse on the divine nature. 147. Praise the Lord, Jerusalem. Praise together with discourse on the divine nature. 148. Praise the Lord from heaven. Praise together with discourse about God. 149. Sing a new song of praise to the Lord. Praise together with prophecy. Praise the Lord in his sanctuary. A general exhortation. A discourse by Didymus on the Psalms in the New Testament. Since words taken from the book of Psalms are cited as testimonies, as from something spoken by the Spirit, Paul, in the letter to the Hebrews, when he takes a passage from the ninety-fourth psalm, writes that this was spoken by the Holy Spirit, saying that the prophet said, “The Holy Spirit says, ‘[?], if you hear his voice,’” and the rest that goes with this. Peter too, the chosen one and chief of the apostles, in the Acts of the Apostles, says things that agree with these. For he says in one place, “The Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus,” and the rest. After adding a few things about these matters, he says, “For it is written in the book of Psalms, ‘Let his dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one living in it,’ and, ‘Let another take his office of oversight.’” It is not strange, however, that the apostles write these things, since the Savior himself confirms them all the more. For when the beginning of the hundred and ninth psalm is mentioned in the Gospel, it reads as follows: “The Lord said to my lord, ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.’” He was asking the Pharisees, “If David, through the Holy Spirit, calls the Messiah ‘Lord,’ how is he his son?” If, then, the psalms contain spiritual meanings, should we not approach their text as it deserves? [?] Discourse on [?] Psalms. Since many of those from the nations who have believed in Christ think that this book belongs to David, and give it the title ‘Psalms of David,’ we must say

these things about it that have come down to us. The Hebrews entitled the book ‘Sefer Tehillim.’ In the Acts of the Apostles, however, it is called the ‘Book of Psalms.’ The wording is as follows: “As it is written in the Book of Psalms.” Here, however, no name is placed in the book’s title. The reason is that the words of one person alone were not written in it; rather, those of many were collected, when Ezra, as the traditions say, gathered the many books of psalms into one after the captivity, or even words that are not necessarily psalms. Thus, at the beginning of one of them David’s name is placed, on another Solomon’s, and on another Asaph’s. Some of them also bear Jeduthun’s name, and besides these there are others, those of the sons of Korah and of Moses. Thus the words of all these were collected together, even though they are called David’s alone, after the one who is well known. But we must inquire about those without titles and whose they are, and not suppose [?]. For why is that heading placed over them which reads ‘Psalms of David’? Or if they are not psalms, there is also the simpler heading that says ‘Of David,’ without any addition. We have supposed, however, that wherever this heading alone occurs, what is spoken is neither a psalm nor a hymn of praise, but a word from the Holy Spirit, written for the benefit of the person who can [?]. A tradition from a certain Hebrew concerning these other psalms has reached me. Since many of them were without titles, and the one preceding these untitled psalms [?] has no heading ‘Of David,’ he used to say that these too, when considered together, should be regarded as David’s. And so, from this point onward, the consequence is that these untitled psalms should belong to the same people as those preceding them, whose attribution is properly understood from the heading. But let us inquire why there are one hundred and fifty. The sacred character of the number fifty among days is known from the very famous Pentecost, which signifies release from labors and joy. For this reason it is not right to fast during these days, or to kneel. For these are signs of [?] the things to come, whose shadow existed in [?] as Israel. Among years, what the Hebrews call the Jubilee is the fiftieth year. Much greater than these is what occurs in these seventh years: the freeing of slaves, the cancellation of debts, and rest from farming and from every labor on the land in that Jubilee year; also, fields and ancestral houses that had been transferred to others because of some worldly need are to return to the family. The sacred Gospel also knows the forgiveness associated with fifty, and speaks of a number of the same kind as it and close to it. For it is not without purpose that fifty is given in boasting [?]. Thus, then, the praises offered to God for the destruction of enemies, and the thanksgiving for God’s help, ought to comprise not just one group of fifty, but three, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. That group of fifty contains seven weeks, seven times seven, and the beginning that follows the final week, in the eighth period of truly new rest. And this, concerning the psalms, [?] very great [?]. Or, in human terms, the words concerning all of them, we may find, as we have set them out, [?] that it is not without purpose that the eighth is entitled ‘Concerning the Winepresses’: it contains the ripening of the fruits in the eighth period. For the time of enjoying the fruits of the vineyard of truth is not yet available. It was to be in the preceding enumeration [?]. That eighth psalm, the second of those concerning the winepresses, is eighth, containing another eightfold number in the tens: namely, the eighty-third. When the number is two, the holy ones who are separated [?]: that of eight in the tens. And that of three in the units, which makes equal [?]. The fiftieth is concerned with forgiveness of sins and confession. For just as the fiftieth, according to the Gospel, has forgiveness of sins in the reckoning concerning the jubilee, so one understands that it is not at another number, but at that fiftieth number, that the person praying receives forgiveness, with such expressions of confession. Again, certain songs of ascent also belong to it, fifteen in number, corresponding to the steps of the temple [?] which comprise ascents, in the number seven and in the number eight. The beginning of the ascent, however, is from that

one hundred and twentieth psalm, which is expressed more plainly, as found in the more accurate copies. This is the number of the full span of human life. And the hundredth, whose opening is, “I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, Lord,” concerns the conduct of the holy person who shares in what comes from God. The one hundred and fiftieth concludes with “Let everything that breathes praise the Lord.” But since, as we said before, concerning each one of them, establishing and praising the reason [?] is very difficult and hard for human nature to comprehend, let these things suffice for us. We add only as an indication that it is not according to the sequence of the biblical history that these psalms, which seem to depend on historical events, were written. And there is a reason for these things, not another [?], or for the number under which the psalms are arranged. For example, the historical event of the fifty-first precedes the historical event of the fiftieth. For the events concerning Doeg the Edomite, who slandered David to Saul, are acknowledged by everyone to precede the sin involving Uriah’s wife. Yet it is not without reason that the event which comes second in history precedes the one which comes first in history, because, as we said before, the passage concerning forgiveness is naturally suited to the fiftieth number. But someone who is unworthy of forgiveness falls beyond the fiftieth number, like Doeg the Edomite. Moreover, the seventy-third, because it was spoken when David was fleeing from the presence of his son Absalom, is known to those who read Kingdoms to come after the fifty-first and after the fiftieth. Such matters, if someone takes greater care to observe the history and examines the headings more closely, enable him to discover the reason for the arrangement of the psalms. Perhaps it has a fourth correspondence [?]. And the fact that David alone among the prophets prophesies with an instrument, which the Greeks call a kinnara and the Hebrews a zabla [?], which alone among musical instruments is straighter than all the others, having nothing curved about it. Nor is its sound produced from the lower parts, as happens with the lyre and certain other instruments, but from above. By Saint Athanasius of Alexandria. A Chapter on the Psalms. The Hebrews divide the whole Book of Psalms into five parts. The first of these comprises those from the first psalm, “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the way of the wicked,” up to the fortieth, “Blessed is the one who considers the poor.” The second comprises those from the forty-first, “Like a deer that cries out for streams of water,” up to the seventy-first, “God, give your judgment to the king.” The third comprises those from the seventy-second, “God is good to Israel, to the pure in heart,” up to the eighty-eighth, “I will sing of the Lord’s mercy forever.” And the fourth comprises those from the eighty-ninth, “Lord, you have been a dwelling place for us throughout our generations,” up to the one hundred and fifth, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his mercy is forever.” The fifth [?] comprises those from the one hundred and sixth, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his mercy is forever,” up to the end of the book. In the Hebrew Book of Psalms they were all written apart from the addition of the numbering [?], and differently: some of them are joined together, while others are divided. Joined together, that is, is the one The first and the second are joined together in Hebrew. Again, the ninth, “I will give thanks to the Lord with all my heart,” which is joined together in our version, is divided into two in Hebrew. The whole book, however, of Psalms is divided into five parts. We must note that the arrangement of the Psalms does not follow the chronological sequence of events, for it is often out of order, as the book of Kings itself shows. For when widespread idol worship took hold of the Jewish people, they neglected their ancestral books, so that the book of the law of Moses could not be found and no memory of the ancestors’ fear of God would be preserved among them. Thus they also killed the prophets who rebuked their evil conduct. Because of these things, they were first handed over to the calamities inflicted by the Assyrians. It is therefore no wonder that, under such conditions, the things contained in the book of Psalms should fall [?] into oblivion and be lost over time.

And again: “Sow righteousness for yourselves and eat the [?] of kindness.” And again: “Look, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send a famine upon the land—not hunger for bread or thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord,” together with the other things in the holy Scriptures that were spoken for the benefit of human beings. You too understand these things, as it is written: “You will all be taught by God.” And if that translation is extensive and too difficult for you, translate what you can—those things that are urgently needed, especially those concerning prayer and virtuous conduct, and how a person should flee from evil and cling to good, and how a person should seek the Lord with all his heart. I ask you in your love that, if it is God’s will and you translate it, a copy of it be sent to us. I would have you know, dear friend, that not one of the saints composed or translated anything without labor. The blessed Mar John, a faithful and trustworthy man and a lover of God, alone translated one or two books, along with the other chapters that were translated from Greek into Syriac, which men translated with great labor out of zeal for God. And now, for our Lord’s sake, labor a little for your brothers and translate what you can, according to your ability, so that by doing this you may receive a blessing from the Lord, and he may forgive all your sins and shortcomings in return for your labor for his holy name. Yes and amen. Give greetings in our Lord to [?] the faithful there, especially those who live with you, and to Mar John, the abbot of Beth Sowa, and those with him, and to Mar Sergius your brother, and to the whole community of your brothers. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself preserve you in his mercy, [?] good for your departed, and mercy and compassion upon your living, through the prayers of the prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and teachers of the truth, and of our Lady Mary, who gave birth to God in her virginity. Yes and amen. Be well in our Lord at all times, [?] that you have. Our brother, lover of God, pray for my lowliness. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Yes and amen.
